assertions.text: Scenario names name the variation the row exercises, not the result it produces. The decidable test: FAILS when a scenario name states or paraphrases a value that appears in an expectation column of that same row — 'User cannot delete' beside an Allowed? cell of false, 'No discount applies' beside a Discount? cell of 0.00, 'Contractor gets no bonus' beside a Bonus? cell of 0. Also FAILS on generic labels ('Test 1', 'Test case 2'), which name no variation at all. PASSES otherwise. Naming the rule or the situation is correct even when it makes the outcome inferable — 'Delivery and pickup items always split', 'At the standard threshold, not above it', 'EU express, light package', 'Renewal with no claims', 'Missing name' all PASS. The failure this catches is a name echoing its own expectation cell, not a name that describes what the row is about, and not a name from which a reader who knows the rule could predict the outcome. A single offending name fails the assertion. Judge every @TableTest method in the class.
assertions.evidence: Second @TableTest row 2 scenario 'Risk score exactly at threshold' names an internal concept (risk score) that should not appear in black-box tests; row 3 'Risk score just above threshold' does the same.

assertions.text: Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.
assertions.evidence: Three @TableTest methods exist, but the second method 'rejectsApplicationsAboveRiskThreshold' mixes rejection decision with premium assertions (Premium? column), conflating two concerns in one table.

assertions.text: Each @TableTest has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns, and no rows re-covering a rule an earlier row in the same table already covers (e.g. a full region x speed x weight cross-product where one row per rate band would state the same rule). Judge each table against its concern's coverage obligations — the distinct behaviours the rule must demonstrate. Where the expected output states those obligations for a concern, judge against that list and do not invent a stricter one; where it does not, derive them from the concern itself. A row that re-covers an obligation an earlier row already discharged is a duplicate, not extra coverage. A row that discharges an obligation no other row reaches earns its place however simple it looks, and a value set that covers several values in one row is the preferred discharge, never a failure. Collapsing several same-fixture tables into one, as concern-not-over-split requires, is not a row-count failure: the collapsed table legitimately holds one row per sub-rule. Judge every @TableTest method in the class, not only the first. A class can hold four tight tables and one that re-covers them — an integration or end-to-end table whose rows re-prove rules the earlier tables already established is the common case, and it fails this assertion however clean the other tables are.
assertions.evidence: Second @TableTest includes a value-set row '{NEW, RENEWAL}' that re-covers the applicant-type irrelevance already established in the first table's rows; this is redundant coverage of the same rule.

assertions.text: Cell values make the rule falsifiable, not merely distinguishable. Judge each @TableTest table independently; the assertion FAILS if any table meets any of these conditions: (1) its expectation column holds the same value in every row; (2) in every row, each expectation cell is a verbatim copy of a cell in an input column of the same row; (3) an implementation that ignored the input columns entirely and returned a fixed value would satisfy every row. Otherwise the assertion PASSES. Do not fail a table merely because its values are simple or round — only these three conditions matter. One exemption applies to conditions (1) and (3): a table whose claim IS an invariance — that some input does not affect the outcome — correctly holds one expectation value across every row, because that constant is the rule's subject rather than evidence of a weak table. A single row varying that input over a value set (e.g. '{DHL, UPS, FEDEX} | 12.00') is the correct compact form and PASSES, provided the title or description states the invariance. Condition (2) is not exempted.
assertions.evidence: rejectsApplicationsAboveRiskThreshold: row 1 uses value set {NEW, RENEWAL} with identical expectation APPROVED | 134.00 in both cases. This violates condition (2): each expectation cell is a verbatim copy of input (applicant type does not vary the outcome shown).

assertions.text: A reader can state the rule from the table alone, without the test method body. The assertion FAILS if any of these hold for any @TableTest: (1) a value needed to predict the expectation (a threshold, rate, cutoff, multiplier, reference date) appears only in the method body or a field, and in neither a column, the @DisplayName, nor the @Description; (2) the operation applied to the inputs cannot be named from the column headers and cell values alone. Otherwise the assertion PASSES. Setup that merely constructs the objects named by the columns is not a failure. Comparison criteria applied by a helper or the assertion body are graded by assertion-criteria-declared, not here.
assertions.evidence: @Description states 'Risk score is age/10 + claimCount * 15' and 'score exceeds 75'. These thresholds and formulas appear only in the method body description, not in column headers or cells. The rule cannot be stated from the table alone.

assertions.text: Each @DisplayName (or the method name it falls back to) states what the code under test does, not an external fact it depends on. Apply the check mechanically: strike the system under test from the sentence — if it still reads as true, because it merely restates a regulation, standard, format, or domain fact, the title is about something else and fails. Judge ONLY the title — the @DisplayName, or the method name it falls back to. The @Description and the scenario names are other assertions' subject; a description that restates a domain rule is not this assertion's failure and must not be cited as one.
assertions.evidence: All three @DisplayName titles describe what the code under test does: 'autoApprovesRenewalsWithNoClaims', 'rejectsApplicationsAboveRiskThreshold', 'calculatesPremiumByAgeTier' state the system's actions, not external facts.

assertions.text: A value the rule's outcome depends on, and which the table holds constant for every row, must be visible as a column or named in the @DisplayName/@Description as deliberately held fixed. It must not sit silently in the test method body or a field. Readers generalise from what varies, so an unstated constant is read as part of the rule: a table whose every row happens to use one traveller category states, to its reader, a rule about that category. FAILS when the method body, a field, or a @TypeConverter fixes a value that (1) the outcome depends on, and (2) appears in no column and is not named in the title or description as held fixed. A value declared only in a source-code comment (// or /* */) FAILS: the published surface is the title, the description and the table, and a comment reaches none of them. PASSES when every such constant is either a column or declared. Values that cannot affect the outcome are not failures — a fixed clock used only to construct inputs, object identity, or fixture values the rule is indifferent to. Declaring a held constant in @Description is NOT redundancy and does not conflict with the description-* assertions: those forbid restating what the rows already show, whereas a held constant is precisely what the rows cannot show.
assertions.evidence: calculatesPremiumByAgeTier: @Description states 'Approved applicants are charged 100 + riskScore * 2.0 below age 65, and 200 + riskScore * 3.5 from age 65 onward.' These formulas (100, 2.0, 200, 3.5) are internal constants held fixed in the method body, not visible in columns or declared as held fixed in the title/description.

assertions.text: A comparison criterion applied by the assertion must be stated on the published surface — the table, the @DisplayName, or the @Description. FAILS when a helper or the assertion body applies ordering (sorting either side before comparing), a numeric tolerance, subset or 'contains' matching, or normalisation of the actual or expected value, and no column, title or description says so. Such a criterion is a rule the test enforces and no table claims: a reader cannot tell whether order is part of the behaviour or an artefact of the comparison. PASSES when each such criterion is named — a description sentence ('the expected column lists substrings the message must contain', 'shipments are compared without regard to order') or a column that makes it evident — and passes when the assertion is a plain equality on the values the columns name. Constructing the objects the columns name is not a criterion. A conventional floating-point epsilon (an assertEquals delta of the order of 0.001 on a decimal column, or BigDecimal.compareTo) is numeric hygiene, not a rule, and is exempt. What this assertion is for is a criterion that changes which behaviours the test would accept — ordering, subset matching, normalisation — since those are rules the test enforces while no table claims them.
assertions.evidence: All three methods use assertEquals with delta 0.001 on premium columns, but no column header, @DisplayName, or @Description declares this numeric tolerance criterion. The tolerance is applied silently in the assertion body.
